n: Dinah, Jacob’s daughter by Leah, goes out to visit the young women of the region. This painful chapter shows the dangers of living among the Canaanites and the family’s struggle to respond rightly to evil.
Shechem, the son of the local ruler, sees Dinah, seizes her, and rapes her. The verbs—took, lay, defiled—describe violence and humiliation.

f.g: One of the peoples of Canaan (10:17).
Humbled or violated—the Hebrew word describes forced, degrading treatment.

n: Afterward Shechem becomes attached to Dinah and speaks tenderly to her. His feelings, however, do not undo the wrong he committed.
Shechem demands that his father obtain Dinah for him as a wife.

f.w: Get me this damsel to wife
f.g: His blunt demand mirrors his earlier taking (compare Judges 14:2).

n: Jacob hears what happened but stays silent until his sons return from the fields. His silence may be caution—or a troubling passivity.
Hamor, Shechem’s father, comes to negotiate with Jacob.
Jacob’s sons return, grieved and furious. The narrator calls the crime an outrage “in Israel”—a disgraceful act that should never be done.

f.g: Committed a disgraceful outrage; a phrase used later for grave sexual crimes (Deuteronomy 22:21; 2 Samuel 13:12).

n: Hamor asks for Dinah as Shechem’s wife but offers no apology for the crime.
Hamor proposes broad intermarriage between the two peoples. This would have dissolved the covenant family into Canaanite society.
He offers land, trade, and property rights—an attractive offer for a wandering family.
Shechem asks for favor and promises to give whatever they ask.

f.w: Let me find grace in your eyes
f.g: Please look kindly on my request.

n: He offers to pay any bride-price and gift they name, as long as he can marry Dinah.

f.g: Bride-price paid to the bride’s family.

n: Jacob’s sons answer deceitfully because of what was done to their sister. Their response sets a trap.

f.g: With cunning or treachery; the same root used of Jacob’s earlier deceit (27:35).

n: They say they cannot give their sister to an uncircumcised man. They misuse the sacred covenant sign as a tool for revenge.
They demand that every male in the city be circumcised as a condition.

f.w: If ye will be as we be

n: If so, they promise to intermarry and become one people—a false promise.

f.g: A promise they never intend to keep.

n: Otherwise, they will take “our daughter” and go. Dinah apparently remains in Shechem’s house (verse 26).

f.g: Dinah, still held in Shechem’s house.

n: Hamor and Shechem are pleased with the terms.
Shechem acts without delay because of his desire for Dinah. He is described as the most respected member of his family.
Hamor and Shechem address the men at the city gate, where public decisions were made.

f.g: The place of public assembly and decisions.

n: They present Jacob’s family as peaceful and the land as roomy enough for everyone.
They explain the one condition: circumcision for every male.
They also appeal to greed: Jacob’s wealth will become theirs. Both sides are bargaining with hidden motives.

f.w: Shall not their cattle and their substance and every beast of theirs be ours?

n: All the men of the city agree, and every male is circumcised.

f.w: all that went out of the gate
f.g: All the men of the city who had civic rights.

n: On the third day, while the men are in pain and weak, Simeon and Levi—Dinah’s full brothers—attack the city and kill all the males. Their revenge is far beyond justice.
They kill Hamor and Shechem and take Dinah from Shechem’s house.

f.w: with the edge of the sword

n: Jacob’s other sons plunder the city, justifying it by their sister’s defilement.
They take the flocks, herds, donkeys, and everything in the city and fields.

f.w: that which was in the field
f.g: Everything outside the city as well.

n: They even take the women and children captive. The wrong done to Dinah has led to far greater violence.
Jacob rebukes Simeon and Levi, fearing their actions have made the family hated and vulnerable to attack. His concern focuses on safety; later he condemns their violence more strongly.

f.g: To make me hated; to give me a bad reputation.

n: The brothers answer with a pointed question: should their sister be treated like a prostitute? The chapter ends without resolution, leaving readers to weigh justice, anger, and mercy.
